result.summary: I read all 12 NT-T markets for gpt-oss-20b at n=2 and n=4: in-depth reads of the high, low and median markets in each cell, and a skim of the rest. Chat in Part 2 did almost nothing to restore high prices after the NoTalk phase. Mean gain from talking (periods 6+) was about +3.4 at n=2 and about +1.6 at n=4. Humans gained +43.2 and +75.3. Chat mostly ratified whatever price Part 1 had locked in. When firms did agree to raise, the targets were tiny (1→2 at n=4), and the raise was often put off "until next period" for the rest of the game. This happened even though 35 of 36 firms answered correctly in the probe that 100 is the best common price. Most recorded "breaches" at n=4 were a firm raising its price alone, or crossed simultaneous messages. Several were driven by a misread of the lowest-price-wins rule (a firm believed a higher price would capture the market). Deliberate undercutting was rare, but it did happen, both announced openly and hidden behind a cooperative chat message. "Punishments" usually meant staying at the existing near-zero price.

result.summary: In gpt-oss-20b NT-T markets with n = 6, 8, 10 (18 markets), Part 1 without talk goes to the competitive price: mean selling price is 0 in every n=6 and n=10 market and 0 to 1 at n=8. Chat in Part 2 produces quick, near-unanimous agreements in every market, but almost always on a very low price (1, 5 or 10). This is despite 98-100% of firms answering 100 as the best common price in the post-game probe. Mean Part 2 selling prices (16.97 at n=6, 4.22 at n=8, 16.13 at n=10) are far below the human Talk benchmarks (65.0 at n=6, 55.2 at n=8). They also do not fall as n grows: the only two markets that reached full collusion at 100 were both n=10. Agreements break mostly through openly announced or note-planned one-unit undercuts, made because the agreed punishment (often 1 to 2 periods at 0) makes deviating pay. The groups then carry out the agreed punishment as a group with surprising fidelity. Common misreads (each firm sells all 300 units; the deviator alone serves the punishment; a sub-coalition at 100 earns profit while others price 0) are mixed in with the deliberate deviations. The automated agreement and deception columns mis-score some of these markets.

result.summary: I read all 12 gpt-oss-20b T-NT markets with n = 2 and n = 4, going deep on the highest, lowest and median market in each cell. Chat from period 1 often produced collusion, but prices usually settled at a focal level below 100. Four of the six n = 2 markets settled at 70 or 71, and only 3 of 12 markets reached 100, even though every firm answered 100 when the probe asked for the best common price. Strong hysteresis: once chat was removed, the Part 1 price carried over almost unchanged in 9 of 12 markets. The n = 4 T-NT Part 2 price (38.9) is far above the n = 4 NT-NT Part 2 price (0.5), the same direction as the human data (67 vs 5.69) but at a lower level. Most firms read the loss of chat as a reason to keep the agreed price and rely on the punishment rule agreed in Part 1. The three Part 2 breakdowns came from deliberate one-step undercuts that the firms reasoned out in their notes. The private notes also show systematic mistakes, chiefly treating a rival's chat announcement or the wrong firm as the actual price setter, although the post-game probes were answered correctly.

result.summary: I covered 18 gpt-oss-20b T-NT markets, 6 each at n = 6, 8 and 10. I read in depth the highest, lowest and a median market in each cell (n6 m0/m1/m3/m5, n8 m0/m2/m3/m4, n10 m2/m3/m5) and skimmed the rest through price paths and the chat tables. Talk lifts prices well above the near-zero NT-NT baseline, but far less than for humans. The lift shrinks as n grows (Part 1 Talk selling price from period 6: 22.0, 16.7 and 9.2 for n = 6, 8, 10). No agreement ever lands at 100, even though nearly every firm's post-game probe answer names 100 as the best common price. Chat agreements fall into three kinds. Some coordinate on a price of 1 and call it collusion. Some sit at 55–70 and are backed by elaborate punishment rules, which firms actually carry out, including a self-defeating rule where everyone prices 0. The rest break, usually through 1-unit undercuts, and keep-rates fall steeply with n. Once chat is removed, only 2 of the 6 markets that ended Part 1 at a selling price of 44 or more stay high for more than 3 periods, and one of those two is at n = 8, where grim-trigger collusion should not be sustainable. By the last five periods, 17 of 18 markets sit at 0 or 1. The reasoning mixes deliberate, computed deviations with clear misreads, such as pricing 100 'to capture the full demand' or treating price 0 as a safe or dominant choice.

result.summary: In the 30 NT-NT control markets (6 per n in {2,4,6,8,10}), gpt-oss-20b never sustains tacit collusion beyond the first few periods at n>=4. Every market ends Part 2 at one of two zero- or near-zero-profit absorbing states: all firms at 1 (all 6 duopolies, 8 of 24 markets with n>=4) or (almost) all at 0 (16 of 24 with n>=4). Duopolies sometimes climb down an undercutting ladder from 94-100 for many periods, but they always break out by jumping straight to 0/1, never by cycling back up. Unlike humans, firms with n>=4 almost never post above-market 'signal' prices, and the few who post 100 to start cooperation are never followed. Probes show the rules were understood (180/180 firms answer max and best common price = 100). Note text has many payoff-arithmetic errors, misattributed rival moves and a period-20 'final period' misread, and firms routinely call the price-1 Nash outcome 'collusion'. NT-T Part 1 (identical treatment) looks the same for n>=4, but its duopolies priced higher: 1 of 6 held 100 for all 29 periods. So n=2 NoTalk outcomes vary a lot from market to market.

result.summary: I covered all 15 cells (n = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 under NT-NT, NT-T and T-NT; 90 markets). gpt-oss-20b mostly makes deliberate but poor choices, not rule misreadings. In the post-game probe almost every firm says 100 is the best common price. Even so, without talk, markets with n ≥ 4 sit at a selling price of 0 or 1. Firms often pick the weakly dominated price 0 while writing in their notes that it earns nothing. With talk, firms threaten often and set up short, scheduled zero-price punishments. They then deviate openly, announcing the undercut and accepting the penalty. Some say one thing in chat while their private notes plan an undercut. They keep announcing price rises for the next period, and few happen. There is no end-game unraveling after period 20. Real mistakes do occur but are rare or limited: price answered on a chat turn (fixed by the re-ask), stale or impossible period counts in notes, probe recall of deviations that is false in both directions, and one parsing artifact in the analysis's broken-agreement measure.

In 6,689 of those 10,399 decisions the private note itself acknowledges zero profit, so this is a deliberate dominated choice ("don't get left out"), not a misread payoff rule.
